profit-maximization-s1.title: Marlowe Mug Works: output and total cost at a price of \$20

table.caption: Daily total cost of a pottery that sells every mug at \$20, the price in a large market it cannot change (invented data for practice)

profit-maximization-s2.title: A firm's cost curves and the price it sells at

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal cost of the sixth mug, in dollars?

why.correct: Marginal cost = change in total cost / change in output = $\frac{116 - 92}{6 - 5} = 24$ dollars.

mistakes.why: That is the average total cost of six mugs (116 / 6). Marginal cost is the change in total cost per added mug.
That is the total cost of six mugs. Subtract the total cost of five: 116 - 92.

items.q: Use the table. How many mugs a day maximize the firm's profit?

why.correct: Each mug adds \$20 to revenue (MR = \$20). MC is 12, 8, 10, 14, 18, 24 and 30. The fifth mug is the last with MR ≥ MC (20 ≥ 18); the sixth costs 24 > 20. Produce 5 mugs.

mistakes.why: The sixth mug costs \$24 to make and sells for \$20, so making it lowers profit by \$4. Stop at the last mug whose MR is at least its MC.
Marginal cost is lowest at two mugs, but mugs three to five still add more to revenue (\$20 each) than to cost.

items.q: Use the table. What is the firm's profit at its profit-maximizing output, in dollars?

why.correct: Profit = TR - TC = $20 \times 5 - 92 = 8$ dollars, the same as $(20 - 18.4) \times 5 = 8$ using ATC = 92 / 5 = 18.4.

mistakes.why: That is total revenue. Subtract total cost, \$92.
That is the gain on the fifth mug alone (MR - MC). Profit is total revenue minus total cost for all five mugs.

items.q: Use the table. Why should the firm not make a sixth mug?
options: Total cost rises when the sixth mug is made
Average total cost is above the price at six mugs
Its MC (\$24) is above its MR (\$20)
Marginal cost is rising at six mugs

why.correct: Compare the margin: the sixth mug adds \$20 to revenue and \$24 to cost, so profit falls by \$4. Stop where MR = MC, or at the last unit with MR ≥ MC.
options: Total cost rises with every mug; the test is whether it rises by more than revenue.
ATC at six mugs is about \$19.33, below the \$20 price; the test is MR against MC.
Right: the sixth mug lowers profit by \$4.
MC is already rising from the third mug, and mugs four and five still add profit.

items.q: Use the table. What is the firm's average revenue when it sells 5 mugs?
options: \$20, the price of each mug
\$100, the revenue from five mugs
\$18.40, the cost of a mug on average
\$8, the profit from five mugs

why.correct: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity. When every unit sells at the same price, AR = MR = P = \$20.
options: Right: AR = TR / Q = 100 / 5 = 20, the price.
That is total revenue; divide by the five mugs.
That is average total cost (92 / 5).
That is profit, not revenue per mug.

items.q: In the graph, the firm sells every unit at the price shown by the horizontal line. At which output does it maximize profit?
options: Where ATC is at its lowest point
Where MC is at its lowest point
Where the price line meets ATC on the right
Where the price line crosses rising MC

why.correct: The horizontal line is d = MR = AR = P. Profit is largest where MR = MC, on the rising part of MC.
options: That minimizes cost per unit, not profit; at this price more output adds to profit.
Past that point, units still add more to revenue than to cost.
Profit is zero there; the firm has gone too far.
Right: there MR = MC.

items.q: In the graph, which area shows the firm's profit at its profit-maximizing output, q*?
options: The rectangle from the price down to zero, from zero to q*
The rectangle from the price down to ATC, from zero to q*
The rectangle from ATC down to zero, from zero to q*
The area between the price line and MC

why.correct: Profit = TR - TC = (P - ATC) x q*. On the graph it is the rectangle between the price and ATC at q*, out to q*.
options: That is total revenue.
Right: profit = (P - ATC) x q*.
That is total cost.
Profit uses ATC, the cost per unit, not MC.

items.q: In the graph, the price falls until the price line just touches the lowest point of ATC. The firm's best output now earns
options: a profit, because MR still equals MC
zero economic profit: price equals ATC
a loss, because the price fell
a profit, because MC is below the price

why.correct: Where the price line touches the bottom of ATC, MR = MC there and P = ATC, so economic profit is zero: the break-even point.
options: MR = MC gives the best output, but at that output P = ATC, so profit is zero.
Right: P = ATC, so revenue just covers every cost, a normal profit.
The price is still high enough to cover ATC at that output.
At the new best output MC equals the price.

items.q: The firm sells at a price set in a large market. Label the axes and the curves of the firm's graph, including its demand curve.

why.correct: Price and cost on the vertical axis, quantity of output across. The horizontal line is d = MR = AR = P: every unit sells at P, so P is the firm's demand, its average revenue and its marginal revenue.

items.q: The left panel shows the market; the firm in the right panel sells every unit at the market price. Mark the firm's profit-maximizing quantity on its demand curve.

why.correct: The firm's demand is the horizontal line at the market price, d = MR = AR = P. It produces where that line crosses MC: MR = MC.
Profit is the rectangle between the price (top edge) and ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity (bottom edge), from zero to that quantity.

slips.tr: That is total revenue, out from zero to the price. Profit is only the part above ATC.

items.q: Draw the firm's demand curve at the price set in the market panel.

why.correct: The firm sells as much as it wants at the market price, so its demand is a horizontal line at that price: d = MR = AR = P.

options: total revenue divided by the quantity sold
total revenue minus total cost
the price times the quantity sold
the extra revenue from one more unit

why.correct: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit sold: the change in total revenue divided by the change in quantity.
options: That is average revenue.
That is profit.
That is total revenue.
Right: MR = ΔTR / ΔQ.

items.q: A firm's total revenue rises from \$400 to \$460 when it sells 25 units instead of 20. What is its marginal revenue per unit, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the change in total revenue for all 5 units. Divide by the change in quantity, 5.
That is average revenue at 25 units (460 / 25). Marginal revenue uses the changes.

items.q: At a firm's current output, marginal revenue is \$15 and marginal cost is \$11. To raise profit, the firm should
options: produce more, as MR exceeds MC
produce less, because cost is rising
keep output the same, because it earns a profit
raise its price above \$15

why.correct: While MR > MC, each extra unit adds MR - MC to profit. The firm expands until MR = MC.
options: Right: MR > MC, so more output raises profit.
Rising cost matters only when it passes MR; here MR is still larger.
Profit is not yet as large as it can be while MR > MC.
The question is about output at the given price.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: why does a firm produce where MR = MC? Fill in each blank.

why.correct: The marginal rule: produce every unit whose marginal revenue is at least its marginal cost, which ends where MR = MC.

specific.frame: Below that output each unit adds ___ to revenue than to cost, so producing it raises profit; above it each unit adds ___ to cost than to revenue, so profit ___.

below.label: Below the output
options: more
less

why.1: Below the output where MR = MC, MR is greater than MC, so units add more to revenue.

above.label: Above the output
options: more
less

why.1: Above it, MC is greater than MR, so units add more to cost.

profit.label: Profit
options: falls
rises

why.1: A unit that adds more to cost than to revenue lowers profit.

specific.model: Below that output each unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so producing it raises profit; above it each unit adds more to cost than to revenue, so profit falls. Profit is greatest where MR = MC because no unit is left that would raise it.

items.q: A firm sells 200 units at a price of \$12. Its average total cost at that output is \$9. What is its profit, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the profit on each unit. Multiply by the 200 units.
That is total revenue. Subtract total cost, 9 x 200 = 1,800.

items.q: A firm sells every unit at the same price and produces where MR = MC. Which statements must hold at that output? Select all that apply.
options: Producing one more unit would add more to cost than to revenue
Price equals marginal cost
Average total cost is at its lowest point
Marginal cost is at its lowest point

why.correct: At the profit-maximizing output MR = MC, and with a constant price MR = P. That output is not where any cost curve bottoms out.
options: True: past that output MC is above MR.
True: when every unit sells at the same price, MR = P, so P equals MC there.
False: the best output depends on the price; it is at the lowest point of ATC only when P = ATC there.
False: the firm produces on the rising part of MC.
